What should I do?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Let's pivot to the BS in Computer Science Games - it's still game-focused but gives you the flexibility you need. As a BS degree, you can take courses across schools, potentially double major, and still work on game development. Plus, this major is eligible for early action on November 1st, while the BFA would require waiting until December 1st. For your second and third choice majors, consider Media Arts and Practice and Journalism. This strategy keeps you competitive for game development while maintaining interdisciplinary options. The key insight: USC specifically emphasizes students can do 'more than one thing' - but that's harder with a BFA. The BS path lets you explore game development while keeping doors open to combine it with entrepreneurship, media, or other interests. Your parents are right to want flexibility - college is for exploration, and you don't want to lock yourself into a narrow path before you've had a chance to discover all your interests."} ], "metadata": { "intelligence_type": "major_flexibility_strategy", "week": "050", "quality_score": 9 } }, { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "Help a student whose team became more productive after a key member quit. My VP is suddenly really active and we went from 50 to 95 Instagram followers. How do I keep this energy going?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Your secretary quitting created a catalyst moment - it forced everyone to realize they need to step up or the organization fails. This is actually common; sometimes losing dead weight energizes the remaining team. To maintain momentum: First, use the urgency. You're all rising seniors - remind everyone that this is their last chance for demonstrated impact before college apps. Second, redistribute the secretary's best tasks to your most engaged members, giving them new titles if needed. Your VP stepping up shows they want more responsibility. Third, celebrate the 95 followers publicly in Slack - you're about to hit 100, which is a psychological milestone. Make it an event. Fourth, set consequences like you did before: 'If tasks aren't done by X date, we need to discuss your role.' The threat of losing their position motivates action. Finally, leverage summer break while everyone has time. Once school starts, this window closes. The key insight: your team discovered they CAN succeed without that person, which is empowering. They're not working harder despite the loss - they're working harder because of it. Keep referencing how much progress you've made since the change."} ], "metadata": { "intelligence_type": "team_catalyst_management", "week": "050", "quality_score": 8 } }, { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "A student discovered that free programs aren't taken seriously and wants to implement a payment model for their nonprofit bootcamp."}, {"role": "user", "content": "We offered a free AI bootcamp and people signed up but didn't show up or take it seriously. Now we want to charge money but we're a student nonprofit. How do we make paid programs work?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You've discovered a fundamental truth: people don't value what they don't pay for. Here's how to implement a payment model: First, get your 501 status immediately - this legitimizes charging fees and allows tax-deductible donations. Second, price it low but meaningful - even $25-50 creates psychological investment. Frame it as a 'program fee' that covers materials and supports your mission. Third, offer scholarships for those who truly can't pay, but make them apply for it - the application process creates investment too. Fourth, donate excess funds to an AI education cause - this makes parents more willing to pay knowing it's for charity. 'All proceeds support AI education for underserved communities.' Fifth, create value markers: certificate of completion, LinkedIn badge, letter of recommendation for engaged participants. People need to see what they're buying. The game development camp for young girls is perfect for this model - parents will pay for quality STEM education. Start with a 2-day pilot program at $50, limit to 10 students, and make it excellent. Success with a small paid cohort beats failure with a large free one.
